content.summary_of_the_paper:
Following Li et al. (2021b), this paper proposed modification for predictive visual  tracking (PVT) method.  Given a frame t recorded, the process time required to process this frame will delay the downstream process and may cause accuracy drop for the current time frame. 
Li et al. (2021b) proposed to benchmark tracking methods with Latency-aware evaluation (LAE). 

This paper follows this evaluation and introduced a sigma parameter to distinguish more on 'real-time' methods with different latency. Instead of use motion prediction from Kalman filter [1], this paper proposed to use motion and appearance information to do predictive tracking. More specifically encode averaged motion from past N frames and feature representation to predict the location of current time frame.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Experiments demonstrated the the proposed motion and appearance combination performs better than the baseline that is the current tracking method without  predictive tracking. Different frame rate, 21f/s, 5f/s, 12f/s and feature dimension are compared.  Also compared and outperformed Kalman based method in Li et al., 2020b

- Given this paper is based on Li et al. (2021b), the baseline method should be Li et al. (2021b), instead of current tracking method without predictive traking.
- To fairly compare with Li et al. (2021b
    * why not test on other frame rate, e.g. 30f/s? which frame rate used in Table 5 while compare with Li et al., 2020b?
    * In table 5,  instead of use average mAUC and mDP over four datasets, performance for individual dataset should be reported. For instance,  table III in Li et al. (2021b reported good performance on DTB70, it would be interesting to compare this modified method with Li et al. (2021b on DTB70 specifically.
- missing discussion regarding the design of the layers for motion, appearance and combining feature module.
- discuss and visualise the improved case with a few frames should be added.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The technical details are mostly covered in the paper. Some discussion missing regarding the layer design for motion and appearance encoding and feature fusion. 

Use motion and appearance combined is not new for object tracking task. Novelty is limited.

Experiments are clear with parameters given. It is possible to reproduce. Code is not available.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This paper proposed to follow the predictive visual tracking concept proposed in Li et al., 2020b and Li et al., 2021b. Instead of use only motion in Kalman filter, this paper proposed to combine motion and appearance for predictive tracking. Experiments demonstrated the improvement over original tracking methods that do not have predictive tracking at all. 

Experiments compare to the proper baseline on individual dataset used in Li et al., 2021b are missing. Discussion regarding the module design for motion and appearance feature encoding and fusion are missing.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studied latency-aware predictive visual tracking targeted on UAV aerial tracking. Due to the processing time of a visual tracker, not matter fast or slow, a predictor shall be applied to the tracking results to compensate for the processing time and produce a real-time results for the current frame. The paper proposed an end-to-end predictive visual tracking (PVT++) which adds an online predictor to any existing visual tracker. This predictor takes the previous motion estimation results and object templates/features from the backbone of the visual tracker to train additional encoder-decoder networks as shown in Fig.3. The paper also extended the benchmark for latency-aware predictive tracking. The proposed PVT++ has been trained on VID, LaSOT and GOT1K and tested on several UAV tracking datasets.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is motivated by the practical real-time requirement by UAV aerial tracking. The proposed additional predictor networks are new and reasonably approach to jointly learning from both motion and appearance features. The proposed method is extensively evaluated on several public UAV tracking datasets.

Some technical details need to be clarified regarding to the training and inference of the proposed predictor. The PVT++ is trained for individual visual trackers to learn how to compensate the real wall time lapsed due to the processing of the visual tracker. 

1) This processing/tracking time for a given frame may be determined by the number of targets in this frame or how clutter of this frame, e.g., if there are some cascaded structures in the visual tracker. Thus, how much time (or frames) to compensate for one target object may be not just related to the motion and appearance of this object, but also the number of targets and the appearances of all targets and background. It is not clear if the paper assumed tracking a single target or considered the variation of tracking time due to clean or cluttered background. 

2) When applying PVT++ to an embedded system for UAV aerial, the actual tracking time of the visual tracker is determined by the hardware platform or even if there are any other tasks running on the hardware at the same time. So it is not clear the tracking time measured during training can match in actual cases during inference on an embedded system. Or does the training have to be aware of the targeted embedded hardware platform to deploy PVT++ in advance?

As this work was motivated by and focused on a specific application, i.e., real-time UAV tracking. I am not that sure this work is a good match to ICLR audiences. Perhaps CVPR/ICRA may be a better venue for this work.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written. The proposed method appears reasonable and sound. The proposed additional predictor network using motion and visual appearance is somewhat novel. The training of the predictor is not easy to reproduced by other researchers as it correlates with the implementation of the related visual tracker with many training details involved.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is a well motivated application paper with a reasonable solution. Well, some technical details need more explanation and justification. The interested audience in ICLR 2023 may be limited.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1137 by Reviewer zGBW

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper deals with the problem of single object visual tracking. In particular it proposes an add-on to standard trackers to cope with the latency in computation when tracking is done online e.g. on a robot. The add-on predicts the tracking state to time instants in future to compensate the latency. The idea is to go beyond Kalman and to exploit motion and visual features in a Siamese feedforward network. The paper is well structured and written with a throughout empirical evaluation in the appendices.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper tackles a very practical but important problem which goes beyond the tracking task. Latency due to the computational time a tracker needs is very often neglected in research, however when it comes to implementation in systems with specific real-time constraints, such latency might hinder the application of SOTA approaches.
The authors investigate latency originated from the computational complexity of the algorithm and the resources available, however there are other latencies such as from communication and the operating system where the delivery of images for given time instants cannot be guaranteed. Furthermore, latency is here compensated by a predictor which is designed as an add-on to some standard tracker. On the other hand, the authors show results where training of tracker and predictor shows better results than using the predictor as add-on (see the ablation studied section, page 8: "... perform much better than fixing the tracker ...").
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well written and the experiments are well described, conduced and explained. Some notes:
- Eq. 10: should P_MV not be the composition P_M (Eq. 7) o P_V (Eq. 8)?
- Regarding Eq. 9: Might this difficulty come from the fact that the search patches do not incorporate some "positional" encoding which is compensated by inferring motion from it.
- On page 9 writing sigma element of [a : b) is not an appealing math. writing style, e.g. write {0.2i | 0<=i<1}
- Tab. 5 shows that the result of PVT++ is quite dependent on the chosen tracker. AUC varies between 0.5 and 0.38 which is quite significant.
- The discussion mentions a nearly 50% smaller overhead of KF than PVT++. I doubt this result as KF is a very simple and computationally a much more efficient algorithm compared to PVT++.
- You say "which practically eliminates onboard latency" in the discussion. From the experiments, one cannot conclude this argument.
- One of the advantages of Kalman filtering is uncertainty estimation. When it comes to latency such uncertainty estimation might be crucial e.g. by estimating the size of the search patches.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My main concern of this work is the limitation of the presented hypotheses and the results for a better understanding of a potentially learned representation in such an online, real-time setting. The authors assume a given tracker so learning the representation of the object is not the aim.
I think the paper misses for this conference to tackle latency in a more general way perhaps by self-supervised, continual learning (see recent work of A. Efros, Berkeley). I recommend to submit this work to a robotics or vision conference.

content.summary_of_the_paper: this paper proposes a visual tracker termed PVT++, a predictive-based tracking. It reviews existing trackers and argues that current works ignore the latency issues for tracking, and propose the tracking + predictive framework. However, in my view, the idea maybe holds, but the proposed framework is not novel. Many works are developed based on such settings. Many typos can be found in this paper and further polishment is needed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
1. the overall structure of this paper seems good. 


Weaknesses: 
1. the related works are listed but have no moderate expansion and evaluation. More detailed introductions to some trackers are needed. 
2. Some writing issues can be easily found, and this paper needs further polishing. 
3. the idea of tracking by predicting is not a novel idea, many works are proposed based on such idea. It is commonly used in tracking task. 
4. the proposed tracking framework is ordinary and featureless. 
5. the claim of "practically eliminates onboard latency." is exaggerated.
